title: Why You Should Pretend Your Most Difficult Students Are Perfectly Well Behaved students-are-perfectly-well-behaved/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that much of difficult students' misbehavior is reinforced by the way teachers treat them differently — hovering nearby, pulling them aside for reminders, or modulating voice and body language around them — all of which function as a form of labeling. He distinguishes between conscious labeling behaviors, like behavior contracts or empty praise, which are relatively easy to stop once a teacher recognizes them, and unconscious ones, like glaring or hovering, which are harder to eliminate. His recommended strategy is to deliberately treat the most challenging students as though they were among the best behaved in the class — smiling, joking, and making eye contact just as with well-behaved students — while still remaining a vigilant observer of all students. He argues this approach can produce visible change within a single day when paired with consistent enforcement of the classroom management plan, and that the deeper, more lasting benefit is internal: students begin to see themselves differently and behave accordingly.
points: Treating difficult students differently — hovering, frequent reminders, modulated tone — functions as a form of labeling that reinforces misbehavior.
Conscious labeling behaviors like behavior contracts and empty praise are easier to eliminate once a teacher becomes aware of them.
Unconscious behaviors like glaring and hovering are harder to stop precisely because teachers often don't realize they're doing them.
Deliberately treating challenging students like well-behaved ones — smiling, joking, eye contact — can produce visible change within a day.
The deepest benefit is internal: students begin to see themselves differently and start behaving in line with that new self-image.
quotes: One of the biggest reasons difficult students misbehave is because they’re often treated with the expectation that they will.
You reinforce the conclusion that they've naturally drawn about themselves that 'behavior problem' is who they are—as much a part of them as their name or eye color.
Labeling has a profound influence on behavior. Yet, a majority of teachers are unaware they're doing it or that it's the primary reason behavior hasn't changed.
If you make a point of pretending that your most challenging students are among the better behaved in the class, then those erroneous beliefs they've been saddled with will start falling away.
When you treat them like everyone else, they begin to feel like a valued member of the class. They begin fulfilling the new prophecy you convey to them through your behavior, words, and actions.
What’s cool about this strategy is that you’ll see a difference within the first day.
Not short-lived improvement, mind you, but change to who they are on the inside. Change that is real, intrinsic, and enduring.
